analysis.one_liner: Restores federal and local authority to regulate cable television rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral and died at the end of the 108th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1996, Congress stripped the FCC and local cable franchising authorities of their power to limit what cable companies could charge. This bill would repeal that 1996 provision and put the older rate-regulation rules from the 1934 Communications Act back in force. Cable subscribers would again have a regulator they could turn to when rates rose. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Telecommunications Subcommittee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that pay for cable television, especially in areas with little competition among cable providers, would gain a check on monthly rate increases. The FCC and local franchising authorities would regain the power to review and limit cable rates as they did before 1996.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 that bars the FCC and local franchising authorities from regulating cable service rates, restoring regulators' authority over pricing.
Reinstates the cable rate regulation provisions of the Communications Act of 1934 as if the 1996 rollback had never been enacted, effective 90 days after passage.

analysis.who_pays: Cable television operators, which would once again face regulator review of their rates and could see caps placed on what they charge subscribers. Shareholders in cable companies would bear any reduction in revenue from regulated rates.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation in the early 1990s was widely criticized as cumbersome and was repealed in 1996 on the theory that growing satellite competition would discipline cable prices; reinstating it could impose regulatory costs and paperwork on cable operators that get passed through to customers.
Caps on cable rates could reduce operators' incentive and cash flow to upgrade networks and expand service, slowing improvements in the nation's cable and broadband infrastructure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give consumers in monopoly cable markets a direct tool against rate increases, which is a real benefit where cable faces no competition. The honest objection is that Congress repealed rate regulation in 1996 expecting competition from satellite and other providers to do the job, and re-regulating could bring back administrative costs and dampen network investment. Whether that tradeoff is worth it depends on how much genuine competition a given local market has, and the bill was never examined in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Telecommunications Subcommittee, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Barney Frank introduced the Cable Consumer Rights Act of 2003 on June 16, 2003, to restore authority the FCC and local franchising authorities lost under the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to regulate cable rates.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced.
Eight days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where it sat for the rest of the Congress.
Nine Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.
The bill received no further action, no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable television operators are better off because the bill died: they remained free from FCC and local rate regulation and kept the pricing freedom Congress gave them in 1996. Cable subscribers gained nothing and continued to face unregulated rates.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate FCC and local authority over cable rates.

for.name: 9 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: House Democrats who signed on as original supporters

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Billy Tauzin (R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; it was never scheduled for a hearing or markup and never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on the bill; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would reinstate rate regulation that the cable industry was freed from in 1996, subjecting its pricing to FCC and local review. Its interest in killing the bill ran directly against subscribers' interest in a check on rates.

industries.industry: Satellite and other multichannel video competitors
industries.note: Regulated cable rates would improve the relative price position of satellite TV providers competing for the same subscribers. The bill did not regulate them directly.
